title: Leaf exposure is changed far more by internode length than by divergence angle

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Leaf exposure is changed far more by internode length than by divergence angle

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: If leaves benefit from being spread apart for exposure to air, lengthening the axis to separate them vertically has a far greater effect than any adjustment of the divergence angle, so the azimuthal 'ideal angle' cannot be the plant's means of optimising exposure.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: then it is surely manifest that the simple way to do so is to elongate the axis, and to set the leaves further apart, lengthways on the stem. This has at once a far more potent effect than any nice manipulation of the “angle of divergence.”

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XIV, “On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis”; topic “Divergence angle and the golden mean”. Scope: leafy shoots of plants

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch14-12: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.60

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The comparative effect can be quantified under explicit physical conditions, but Thompson leaves exposure and biological context underspecified. Existing architectures permit restricted simulation tests rather than a universal conclusion.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Use 3D shoot architectures and radiative-transfer or airflow models to independently vary internode length and divergence angle, measuring marginal changes in light and air exposure. A consistently larger effect of internode elongation supports the prediction; equal or larger divergence effects refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Internode length has costs and functions omitted from the comparison.

Open 3D shoot datasets cover few species.

Model results depend on canopy, sun angle, leaf posture and the definition of exposure.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The comparison Thompson makes is a sensitivity calculation: separating leaves along the stem versus adjusting azimuth. Typical internodes, leaf sizes, and divergences are known from many studies, but they are not one downloadable shoot dataset, and the sunflower file does not represent leafy stems. The geometric inequality can be evaluated for published ranges with standard models; the adaptive conclusion that the ideal angle therefore cannot be the plant's means is a further inference.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In a light-interception model, vary internode length and divergence angle over the ranges seen on leafy shoots and compare the change in mutual shading. The geometric claim is supported if realistic internode changes reduce overlap far more than realistic angle changes; it is refuted if, at observed leaf sizes, angle adjustments move exposure as much as internode changes do.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Divergence angle and internode length are seldom published together as an open shoot-architecture table.

A larger geometric effect on exposure does not by itself show what the plant's developmental means of optimizing light are.
